passage: There is a small puzzle about time that most people have noticed without ever stating it. A week spent travelling somewhere new seems to vanish while it is happening, so that there is never enough of it; yet once the traveller is home, the same week looks enormous, crowded with places and faces, as if it had lasted a month. A week at a familiar desk behaves in the opposite way. It drags while it is lived, each afternoon longer than the last, and then collapses in memory into a single grey item that seems to have taken no time at all.

The puzzle dissolves once we accept that we judge duration in two quite different ways. While an interval is passing, our sense of its length depends largely on how much attention we pay to time itself: boredom draws attention to the clock and stretches the hour, while absorption draws it away and the hour shrinks. Looking back, however, we have no clock to consult. We estimate how long a period lasted from what it left behind, and a period that left many distinct memories is judged to have been long. Novelty therefore works in opposite directions on the two judgements, shortening the interval as experienced and lengthening it as remembered.

This distinction sheds light on a complaint that becomes common in middle age, that the years go faster than they used to. The complaint is almost always retrospective. Few people find that a particular afternoon passes faster at fifty than at fifteen; what they find is that last year, viewed as a whole, seems to have been brief. If remembered duration tracks the number of distinct memories, the explanation is not far to seek, since adult life is more routine than youth, with fewer firsts, and a year of repeated weeks leaves less behind to measure it by.

The account is persuasive, but it should be held loosely. It is unlikely that a single factor explains how time seems at every age, and other changes, in health, in responsibility, in how far ahead people habitually plan, probably play a part. Still less does it follow, as some cheerful advice suggests, that one can lengthen a life simply by filling it with novelty. A crowded year may indeed look longer in retrospect, but it will feel shorter while it is lived, and there is no obvious reason to prefer one of these measures over the other. What the distinction teaches is not a technique for buying time but a caution against speaking of how long something 'really' felt, as though there were only one answer.

passage: The case for an independent central bank is usually made in terms of temptation. Elected governments face voters at regular intervals, and before an election they are tempted to loosen money, buying a brief rise in output and employment at the price of higher inflation later. Because the public comes to anticipate this, it builds the expected inflation into wages and prices in advance, so that the boost to output never materialises and only the inflation remains. Handing monetary policy to an appointed body with a mandate for stable prices removes the temptation and makes promises of low inflation believable. The gain, on this account, lies in credibility rather than in any superior cleverness on the part of the officials.

Against this stands a democratic objection that is easy to underrate. Decisions about interest rates have large effects on the distribution of income and wealth, between borrowers and savers, between the owners of assets and those who live on wages, and between one region and another. In a democracy, choices with consequences of that kind are supposed to be made by people who can be removed at the ballot box. To delegate them, the objection runs, is to take out of public contest exactly the decisions that most need it.

Both positions are partly right, and the distance between them narrows once we ask what, precisely, has been delegated. Independence in the choice of instruments is not the same as independence in the choice of goals. A legislature can fix the target, an inflation rate for instance, and require the central bank to explain in public whenever it misses; that body then decides how to reach the target, and it alone sets the interest rate. This arrangement preserves the commitment that defeats electoral temptation while leaving the ends of policy with elected representatives, and it answers much of the democratic objection without surrendering the gain in credibility.

The settlement is stable, however, only while the mandate remains narrow. When central banks are asked in addition to secure financial stability, support employment, steer credit towards favoured sectors or manage the risks of a changing climate, the claim that they merely apply technical means to democratically chosen ends begins to wear thin, because deciding how to trade these goals off against one another is itself a political judgement. The more a central bank is asked to do, the weaker its claim to be left alone while doing it.

passage: It is natural to think of seeing as a kind of recording. Light enters the eye, an image forms on the retina, and the brain, like a careful clerk, reads off what is there. The picture is attractive because it matches how perception feels: effortless, immediate, and apparently free of any contribution from the perceiver. Yet the retinal image is a poor document: it is upside down, flat, constantly jittering with the movements of the eye, and interrupted by a blind spot where the optic nerve leaves the retina. Above all, it is ambiguous, in the sense that a small image on the retina could be a small object nearby or a large one far away; a patch of dim grey could be a dark surface in bright light or a pale surface in shadow. The eye, in short, delivers considerably less information than we ordinarily experience ourselves as seeing.

For this reason many students of vision have preferred to describe perception as a form of inference. The brain, on this account, treats the incoming signal as evidence and settles on the interpretation that best explains it, given what it has learned about how the world usually is. Light tends to come from above, so a disc shaded darker at the bottom is seen as a bump and the same disc turned over as a dent. Objects tend to keep their size, so a person walking away is seen as receding rather than shrinking. These are not conclusions we reach; they are conclusions reached on our behalf, before anything is presented to awareness.

The word 'inference' invites an obvious objection: if perception is a guess shaped by expectation, why do we not simply see whatever we expect? The answer is that the guess is tightly disciplined by the evidence, and that the expectations doing the work are of a peculiar kind. They are not the beliefs we hold and can revise in conversation, but assumptions built up over a lifetime of looking, and perhaps over the history of the species. This is why many visual illusions survive full knowledge of the trick. A viewer who has measured two lines and found them equal will still see one as longer; what she knows and what she sees have been settled by different processes.

It would be a mistake, then, to conclude that perception is unreliable because it is inferential. The assumptions it relies on are mostly true of the environments in which they were formed, which is why they so rarely mislead us outside the laboratory, where illusions are carefully built to exploit them. What the inferential view really overturns is not our trust in the senses but the idea that seeing is passive. Every glance is a small act of interpretation, and its seeming effortlessness is the mark of how well the work is done, not evidence that no work is being done.

passage: Philosophical discussions of ethics characteristically concentrate on the moment of decision. A situation is described, the available options are set out, and the question is which of them a good person would choose. This framing is natural for the purposes of argument, but it quietly assumes that the morally significant work begins only once the situation has been described. In ordinary life, nobody hands us the description. What we take the situation to be, which features stand out and which recede into the background, is settled largely by what we attend to, and that settling is accomplished before any choice is considered.

Consider a manager who prides herself on her fairness. When a request for leave arrives, she weighs it conscientiously against the requirements of the team, and she applies identical rules to everyone. Yet for months she has failed to notice that one reserved employee has grown withdrawn and anxious, while she registered immediately when a more assertive colleague appeared dissatisfied. Her decisions, examined individually, may be beyond reproach. The defect lies upstream, in a pattern of attention that has made some people's difficulties vivid to her and rendered others' invisible.

It may be objected that this demands too much of ordinary moral agents. Noticing is not something we do at will; we cannot be blamed for failing to perceive what never came to our notice, any more than for failing to hear a sound pitched too high for human ears. There is something genuinely correct in the objection. No single lapse of attention is a choice, and it would be unjust to treat it as though it were. But attention is not fixed in the way the range of hearing is. It is formed by what we have habitually looked for, by whom we have taken seriously, and by the stories we tell ourselves about the people around us, and these are things over which, across time, we have considerable influence.

The upshot is that moral improvement is frequently less a matter of resolving to choose better than of learning to see better. A person who wishes to be fair must ask not only whether her decisions follow sound principles but also whose circumstances reach her as calls for decision at all. This is slower and less dramatic work than heroic choice, and it rarely earns admiration, since what it changes is largely invisible from outside. It is nonetheless where a great deal of moral life actually takes place.

passage: Conservationists have long sorted species into two kinds. Native species belong where they are found and deserve protection; alien species, carried by people beyond their former range, are suspect, and those that spread are labelled invasive and targeted for control. The distinction is so familiar that it is rarely examined, yet it rests on a choice that is not itself ecological. To call a species native is to say that it was present before some date, usually the arrival of a particular wave of human travel or trade, and the date is a convention. Species have always moved, carried by winds, currents and birds or on their own legs, and as the climate warms many are shifting their ranges without any human hand to carry them. A plant that crosses a mountain range by itself is not usually called an invader; one that crosses in a shipment of grain is.

A growing number of ecologists conclude that origin should simply be dropped as a criterion. What matters, they argue, is what a species does. Many introduced species cause no measurable harm, and some are positively useful: they hold soil on eroded slopes, feed pollinators where native flowers have been lost, or provide cover for native birds in landscapes that offer little else. Campaigns to remove such species spend scarce money and can do damage of their own, through herbicides, through disturbance of the ground, or by stripping out shelter on which native animals had come to depend. Judging species by their passports rather than by their effects is, on this view, a kind of ecological nativism, and conservation would do better without it.

The critics are right that origin is not itself a harm, and right that much eradication has been undertaken without asking whether the target was doing any damage. But their alternative assumes that effects can be known at the moment a decision has to be made, and this is often false. Introduced species frequently remain scarce and inconspicuous for decades before something, a change in climate, a new road, the arrival of a suitable pollinator, allows them to spread rapidly. By the time the harm is plain, removal has usually become impossible. Moreover, a newly arrived species has no shared history with the predators, parasites and competitors of its new home, and so its future behaviour there is harder to forecast than that of a species whose relationships have been worked out over a long time. This does not make the newcomer more likely to be harmful; it makes its effects less predictable, which is a different thing.

Seen this way, origin is neither a verdict nor an irrelevance but a piece of evidence, and what it is evidence of is uncertainty. Its weight changes with time. When a species has only just arrived, removal is cheap and its effects are unknown, and a presumption against it is reasonable precisely because the decision cannot wait for the evidence that the critics demand. When a species has been established for a century and its effects can be observed, the presumption has done its work, and the case for removing it should rest on what it is shown to do; the label alien then adds little. Both the defenders of the old distinction and its critics treat the question as one of identity, of what a species is. It is better understood as a question of timing and of knowledge: of what can be known about a species, and when.

passage: When professional scientists first began to rely on volunteers to record birds, butterflies or the timing of spring flowers, the objection most often raised was that amateurs would make mistakes. A trained ornithologist can tell two similar warblers apart by a fragment of song; a weekend walker may not know that there are two species to distinguish. Such worries were not idle, for a single confident error repeated across many records can manufacture a trend that does not exist. Data gathered by such walkers, the argument went, would be riddled with misidentifications, and conclusions drawn from it would be built on sand.

The worry was reasonable, but experience has shown it to be aimed at the lesser target. Well-run projects have learned to ask volunteers for the kinds of observation they can make reliably, such as whether any frog was heard calling at a pond on a given evening, rather than the kinds that demand years of training. Where identification is genuinely hard, volunteers can photograph what they see and leave the naming to specialists, and records that look improbable can be flagged and checked. Errors do not vanish, but when thousands of independent observations are pooled, isolated mistakes tend to be swamped by the many correct reports around them.

The more stubborn problem lies not in what volunteers see but in where and when they look. People record wildlife near their homes, along popular footpaths and on fine weekends, so that their records cluster wherever leisure, access and good weather happen to coincide. They visit nature reserves more often than industrial estates, and gardens more often than farmland. A map of volunteer sightings is therefore partly a map of the species and partly a map of the observers, and no amount of skill in identification will separate the two. A bird that seems to be thriving in the suburbs may simply be living where the watchers live.

This bias is harder to correct than misidentification precisely because it is invisible in any single record. Each observation may be impeccable; the distortion appears only in the pattern. Projects that take it seriously ask some volunteers to survey assigned locations at fixed times, accepting fewer and less convenient records in exchange for a sample whose shape is known. Such schemes demand more of participants, and they rarely attract the crowds that open recording does. But they show that the reliability of citizen science was never really a question about the competence of amateurs. It is a question about whether the people designing a project have thought as carefully about sampling as about skill.

passage: A recurring complaint about modern money holds that it lost its integrity when it ceased to be tied to gold. On this view, a currency backed by metal disciplines governments: they cannot issue what they do not hold, and so savers are protected from the slow erosion of their wealth by inflation. The appeal is easy to understand, since gold is tangible, scarce and ancient, while paper notes and electronic balances seem by comparison to be mere promises, and promises can be broken.

Yet the discipline the gold standard imposed was less a protection than a transfer of risk. Under a metallic standard, the quantity of money depended on the pace of mining and on the flow of metal between countries, neither of which had much to do with the needs of trade. When output grew faster than the stock of gold, prices had to fall, and falling prices are hard on anyone who owes money. A farmer who borrowed against next year's harvest found that the harvest fetched less while the sum he owed stayed exactly the same. Long stretches of gold discipline were therefore stretches in which debtors, who were usually the less wealthy, bore much of the cost of keeping money sound for their creditors.

Nor did the standard remove discretion from governments as completely as its admirers suggest. Countries suspended convertibility during wars and crises, altered the official price of gold, and managed their reserves with a good deal of judgement. The rule held while it was convenient and was set aside when it was not; what it chiefly removed was the ability to respond to a slump without first abandoning the rule itself, and many economic historians have observed that, in the depression of the 1930s, the countries that left gold earlier tended to recover earlier.

None of this means that the nostalgia is groundless. Its real object is not the metal but trust: people want assurance that whoever controls money will not debase it for short-term ends. That is a legitimate demand, and governments have given it plenty of justification, but it is better met by institutions whose conduct can be observed, questioned and corrected than by tying the supply of money to the accidents of geology. Gold offers the comfort of a rule that no one made; the difficulty is that a rule no one made is also a rule that no one can sensibly adjust when circumstances change.

passage: When a market collapses, the verdict arrives quickly: it was a bubble, and those who bought near the top were caught up in a collective madness. The diagnosis is comforting, because it implies that the error was obvious and that sober people would have avoided it. It is also, in a great many cases, a judgement that could have been made only afterwards. A price that later falls by three quarters was not necessarily irrational when it was paid; it may have been a reasonable wager on an outcome that simply did not occur.

Consider the shares of firms built around a genuinely new technology. No one knows at the outset which of them will dominate, how large the market will become, or how long any dominance will last. A high price for the whole group can reflect the small chance of an enormous success for one or two of its members, and when most of them then fail, the collapse in prices is consistent with the original bet having been a sensible one. Hindsight converts uncertainty into folly by forgetting that the winners were not known in advance. The same consideration explains why confident announcements that a bubble is under way have such a mixed record, since prices have sometimes gone on rising for years after the warning was issued.

None of this shows that bubbles are a myth. Something does distinguish a bubble from a failed bet, but it is not the size of the eventual fall; it is the reason for which the asset was bought. A buyer who pays a high price because she believes the asset will yield returns that justify it is making a wager that may be mistaken but is not speculative in the narrow sense. A buyer who pays the price only because he expects someone else to pay more, and who would not hold the asset on its own merits for a day, is taking part in something of a different kind: a chain whose value depends on recruiting a next buyer, and which must at some point break.

The difficulty is that this distinguishing mark lies in motives, and prices do not record motives. Two buyers paying the same price on the same day may be doing quite different things, and an observer who sees only the price cannot tell how much of a market consists of believers and how much of passers-on. That is why proposals that regulators should identify bubbles as they form and deflate them, by raising interest rates or restricting purchases, ask for a judgement that is rarely available in time, and why such measures, if applied, are likely to fall on sound and unsound investments alike.

A more modest aim is within reach. What turns the collapse of a price into a wider calamity is usually not the fall itself but the borrowing that financed the purchases, because losses on borrowed money pass from the buyer to the lender, and from the lender to everyone who depends on it. Limits on leverage do not require anyone to know whether a price is justified; they require only that whoever turns out to be wrong should be wrong mainly with his own money. This is less dramatic than a promise to prick bubbles before they grow, and it will disappoint those who want the next crash prevented rather than contained, but a rule that works without foresight has the considerable merit of not depending on a capacity that no one possesses. Such a policy does not aim to prevent bubbles. It aims to make them survivable.

passage: When people settle an argument about a word by 'looking it up', they treat the dictionary as a court whose ruling ends the case. The image is understandable, since a dictionary speaks in the flat, confident voice of a statute, but it misrepresents how the better dictionaries are made. A serious dictionary does not decide what words mean; it reports, as carefully and as comprehensively as it can, what speakers and writers have been observed to mean by them.

The method is easiest to see in the large historical dictionaries begun in the nineteenth century. Their editors did not sit down and define words from their own sense of correctness. They gathered evidence: slips of paper, many of them sent in by volunteer readers, on each of which a sentence containing a word had been copied out with its source and date. A definition was written only after the slips for a word had been sorted into piles according to the senses they seemed to show. Where the evidence was thin, the entry was thin; where a sense appeared in the slips before anyone had thought to approve of it, it went in regardless. The definition, on this model, is a summary of a body of quotations, and the quotations printed beneath it are not decoration but the grounds on which it rests.

It does not follow that a dictionary is a neutral mirror. The evidence has to be collected by someone, and collectors read some kinds of text more than others; for a long time published literary prose was heavily over-represented, while the speech of the street and the workshop barely appeared. Someone must also decide where one sense ends and another begins, a judgment the slips cannot make for themselves. And the labels a dictionary attaches, such as 'informal', 'nonstandard' or 'archaic', are themselves verdicts, even when they are offered as descriptions. A dictionary that claimed to have no point of view would simply be concealing the one it has.

The honest position lies between the court and the mirror. A good dictionary is an argument from evidence: its claims can be checked against the citations, and they can be revised when new evidence arrives, which is why the best dictionaries are never finished. To read one well is to notice the quotations as well as the definitions, and to treat its authority as that of a careful witness rather than a judge. That is a more modest authority than the one we usually grant it, but it is a sturdier one, since it does not collapse the first time usage moves on.

passage: We tend to judge a portrait by asking whether it captures the person. A good portrait, on this view, reveals something of the sitter's inner life: a habit of mind, a private sorrow, the particular way one face differs from all others. Measured against this standard, many older portraits seem stiff and oddly impersonal. Rows of nobles stand in nearly identical poses, their faces composed into the same calm, their individuality apparently buried beneath velvet and armour. It is easy to conclude that their painters were trying to capture the person and largely failing.

That conclusion mistakes what such portraits were for. For much of the history of European portraiture, and of several other traditions, the purpose of a commissioned portrait was less to record a personality than to establish a position. The sitter appeared as a holder of office, an heir, a bride, the head of a house. Costume, setting and objects carried meanings that contemporaries could read: the chain of a civic office, a dog standing for fidelity, a column suggesting constancy, a distant estate glimpsed through a window. A portrait of this kind was closer to a document than to a confession. Its sameness was not a failure of observation but a deliberate placing of the individual within a recognisable type, since what the patron wished to have recorded was precisely the type he had come to occupy. A contemporary who knew the conventions could read an entire biography of rank in a single canvas, whereas a modern viewer expecting the revelation of a character finds only an inventory of possessions.

Likeness was not irrelevant. Families wanted to know what an absent bride looked like, and painters could be criticised for flattering too much or too little. But likeness served the larger purpose rather than defining it. A face had to be recognisable enough to attach the role to the right person, and beyond that the painter's task was to make the person fit the role. The expectation that a portrait should instead expose the sitter, catching him off guard or revealing what he might prefer to hide, belongs to a later and narrower moment in the genre's history. Where an older portrait does strike modern eyes as startlingly intimate, it is worth asking whether it was made for a public hall or for a private room, since the obligations of display weighed very differently in the two settings.

Several changes made that expectation possible. The growth of a buying public outside courts and great houses created sitters with no office to display. New ideas about the self encouraged the belief that a person's truth lay within rather than in his station. And when photography arrived in the nineteenth century, it soon took over much of the trade in cheap likenesses, leaving painters free, or obliged, to offer something a camera seemed unable to supply. The psychological portrait, in other words, is not the essence of the genre finally achieved but one of its historical forms.

To say this is not to claim that the older portraits had no inner life, or that modern ones are free of display. A shrewd painter could let a sitter's character show through the conventions, and a present-day portrait of a company chairman, with its carefully chosen office and posture, documents a position as surely as any court painting did. The point is only that we should judge a portrait by the question it was asked to answer. Faulting a court painter for failing to reveal a soul is like faulting a map for failing to be a landscape painting.

passage: Geologists divide the history of the Earth into named intervals, and they are unusually strict about where one interval ends and the next begins. A boundary is not fixed by a date written in a textbook but by a physical reference point: a particular layer in a particular sequence of rock or sediment, chosen because it records a change that can be recognised in deposits across the globe, and marked, in the profession's half-joking phrase, by a golden spike. The rigour has a purpose. The time scale exists so that a geologist examining strata on one continent can say with confidence that they formed at the same time as strata on another, and a boundary that cannot be traced from place to place is of little use for that task. Precision about where a boundary lies is, in this sense, the price paid for precision about when.

The proposal that we now live in a new interval, the Anthropocene, defined by the imprint of human activity on the planet, has therefore been argued in unusual terms. Much of the debate has concerned not whether humans have transformed the Earth, a point few specialists now dispute, but where the spike should go. Candidates have ranged from the spread of farming thousands of years ago, through the industrial burning of coal, to the middle of the twentieth century, when fallout from nuclear weapons tests left a thin but nearly worldwide trace in sediments and ice. The later dates are favoured partly because they are sharp. A signal laid down within a few years everywhere is exactly what a stratigrapher wants; the slow spread of farming, which reached different regions in different millennia, is not.

Here the demands of the time scale begin to distort the story they are meant to record. Human influence on the Earth did not arrive at one moment. Forests were cleared, soils eroded and large animals hunted to extinction over thousands of years, at different times on different continents, and the acceleration of the last century was the culmination of that history rather than its beginning. Choosing the mid-twentieth century because its markers are crisp risks implying that the transformation began then, and that everything before it belongs to an untouched natural world. A boundary drawn there would be accurate about the rocks and misleading about the long human history that produced them. The criterion that makes a boundary useful for correlating rocks is not the criterion that makes it faithful to a process that was, by its nature, gradual and uneven.

None of this shows that formal definition is pointless. A ratified boundary would give researchers in many fields a common reference, and it would carry an authority that informal usage lacks. Some defenders of formalisation fear that without it the idea will remain a slogan, borrowed by commentators and never disciplined by evidence. But the concept does not need a spike to do its intellectual work. The claim that human activity has become a force comparable to the processes that build mountains and shift climates rests on measurements of carbon, sediment, species and nitrogen, and those measurements remain what they are whatever any committee decides. A concept can be rigorous without being a unit of the time scale; geologists already speak, informally, of great events that unfolded over long and varying spans. The Anthropocene may be better understood in that way, as a transformation with a long and diachronous history, rather than as an epoch that began in a particular year.

passage: Many of the long novels of the nineteenth century first reached their readers not as books but in instalments, issued monthly or weekly over a year or more, in magazines or in separate parts. Modern criticism has tended to treat this fact as an extenuating circumstance. When such a novel sprawls, introduces a character it later forgets, or closes a chapter on a contrived moment of suspense, the serial is invoked as an excuse: the author was writing to deadline, paid by length, obliged to bring readers back next month. The implication is that the real novel, the one the author would have written in better conditions, lies somewhere beneath the one we have, and that serial publication is a kind of noise to be filtered out.

The trouble with this view is that it treats the serial only as a set of pressures, when it was also a set of possibilities, and many of the qualities we now admire in these books grew from it. A novel read over eighteen months is lived with in a way that a novel read over a week is not. Its characters age alongside their readers; its crises arrive amid the readers' own. The large casts and interwoven plots that later critics found unwieldy were in part a response to this rhythm, since a reader returning after a month's absence needed several lines of interest to pick up, and recurring figures with distinctive habits of speech helped her find her place. What looks in a single volume like digression could, at the pace of first reading, serve as the texture of a world one returned to.

Serial publication also made the novel unusually public while it was still unfinished. An instalment could be discussed before the next was written, and authors could, and sometimes did, adjust their plans in light of how readers responded. A purist may regard this as a surrender of artistic control. It can as easily be seen as a kind of conversation, in which a book took shape partly through its encounter with an audience rather than being delivered complete to readers whose only role was to receive it. For a time the novel became a shared event, followed by readers who knew that a great many others were reading the same pages in the same weeks.

None of this is to deny the costs. Writing to fixed lengths did produce padding, and the demand for suspense at the end of each part did produce cliffhangers that the story did not need and that read awkwardly once the parts were bound together. A reader of the collected volume is entitled to notice these. What deserves suspicion is the standard against which they are judged as failures: the ideal of the novel as a single, unified design, conceived whole and executed according to plan. That ideal has a history of its own, and it gained much of its authority later, among writers and critics who worked for a different market and under different conditions. Applied backward, it does not so much reveal the faults of serial fiction as convert its differences into faults.

There is, finally, an irony in the critical embarrassment. Long television dramas, released in episodes and discussed between them, are now often praised by critics for the very qualities, the slow accumulation, the large cast, the sense of a world lived alongside, that the instalment novel was once thought to need excusing for. Nothing about the newer form proves the older one right, and a slack episode is no better for belonging to a celebrated series. But the shift in judgement suggests that what critics of the instalment novel took for timeless standards of form were, at least in part, the habits of one particular way of reading.

passage: The defence of meritocracy rests on a simple and appealing idea: that positions and rewards should go to those who earn them, through talent and effort, rather than to those born into the right family. Against the background of aristocratic privilege this was a revolutionary thought, and it remains a powerful one. Yet it has been attacked, with increasing force, on the ground that talent and effort are themselves largely matters of luck. No one chooses the abilities they are born with. And the capacity to work hard, to persist through failure and to defer gratification, is shaped by upbringing, health and circumstance in ways that no one controls. If this is so, the critic concludes, nobody deserves the rewards that meritocracy hands out, and the language of merit is a flattering fiction.

The premises of this argument are difficult to deny, but its conclusion moves too fast. It runs together two different claims that a person might make about a reward. One is that she deserves it in a deep moral sense, that the world would be unjust if she did not have it. The other is that she is entitled to it, because she has met the conditions that a fair set of rules laid down in advance. A runner who wins a race under fair conditions is entitled to the prize even if her speed owes much to her genes and her coaching; to take the prize away on the ground that she was lucky would itself be a wrong, because she trained and competed on the understanding that winning would bring it. Entitlement of this kind does not depend on the winner being the author of her own talents. It depends only on the fairness of the rules and her compliance with them.

Seen in this light, a society can reward productive contributions, and honour the expectations its rules create, without pretending that the rewards measure the moral worth of those who receive them. It also leaves open, as it should, the question of whether the rules themselves are fair, including how much inequality of reward they ought to permit. What the luck argument undermines is not the practice of rewarding achievement but a particular story told about it, the story in which the successful have simply earned their place and the unsuccessful have simply failed to earn theirs. That story is corrosive. It encourages the winners to regard their advantages as wholly their own, and it adds to the losers' material disadvantage the further injury of being told that they deserved it. The remedy is not to abolish merit but to hold it more lightly.

passage: The mirror test has an appealing simplicity: an animal is given a mark it cannot see directly, perhaps a spot of odourless dye on the forehead, and is then shown a mirror. If it uses the reflection to inspect or rub at the mark on its own body, it is said to recognise itself. Great apes generally pass, most monkeys generally fail, and over the decades a handful of other species have been reported to pass or nearly pass. Because the result is so easy to state, it has come to be treated as a kind of membership test: those who pass belong among the self-aware, and those who fail are presumed to lack a self worth the name.

The test does measure something real. To pass, an animal must grasp that the moving figure in the glass is not another individual and that what it sees there corresponds to its own body. That is not a trivial achievement, and it is reasonable to think that animals capable of it have some representation of their own bodies as objects among others. The difficulty lies in what is inferred from failure, and in how much is read into success.

Consider failure first, since the test presupposes an animal that relies heavily on vision, that attends to its own appearance, and that is bothered enough by an odd mark to investigate it. Many animals meet none of these conditions. A dog, which navigates its world largely by smell, may simply have no interest in a silent image that gives off no scent; an animal whose species does not groom may see no reason to touch a spot on its skin. Failing a test designed around one animal's priorities is weak evidence that another animal lacks the capacity being tested, in the way that a person's failure to answer a question asked in an unfamiliar language reveals little about her knowledge.

Success is open to over-reading too. Recognising one's body in a mirror shows an understanding of the body as one's own; it does not show, by itself, that the animal reflects on its past, imagines its future or thinks of itself as a person with a history. These are richer capacities, and the leap from the mirror to them is a leap of interpretation, not of evidence. None of this makes the test worthless. It makes it one probe among many, informative within its range and silent outside it. The error is not in running the test but in letting a single, visually biased procedure decide which minds are admitted to the category of the self-aware.

passage: When a language is said to be endangered, the response that attracts the most attention is documentation. Linguists record the last fluent speakers telling stories, explaining how to build a house or prepare a medicine, conjugating verbs on request; the recordings are transcribed, annotated and deposited in archives designed to outlast the people who made them. Such projects are routinely described as saving the language, and the phrase is meant sincerely. Something irreplaceable is, after all, being kept from disappearing.

But what is kept is not quite a language. A language, in the sense that matters to its speakers, is a practice: it is what people do when they greet one another, quarrel, court and console, and its existence consists in the fact that children acquire it from those around them. An archive holds evidence of that practice, often superb evidence, but it no longer holds the practice itself. To say that a recorded language has been saved is a little like saying that a photographed forest has been conserved. The photographs may be invaluable to someone who later tries to replant; they are not the trees.

The distinction would be pedantic if it did not affect what gets done. It does. Documentation produces outputs that funders and universities know how to count: hours of recording, entries in a dictionary, a published grammar. Supporting transmission produces almost nothing of the kind. It means paying for a language nest in which grandparents look after toddlers, defending a family's decision to speak the home language against the advice of a doctor or a teacher, or making it possible for young adults to earn a living without moving to a city where the language is of no use to them. These efforts are slow, uncertain and hard to evaluate, and when resources are short, the countable work tends to win.

None of this is an argument against archives. Where a community later sets out to bring back a language that has ceased to be spoken at home, the quality of the earlier documentation can decide how much of it can be recovered, and descendants have had reason to be grateful for the patience of a recorder who wrote down what their grandparents' generation did not pass on. The mistake is to treat documentation as the rescue rather than as insurance against the rescue failing. Where speakers still exist and children could still learn from them, the record is the second-best outcome, and a policy that spends most of its effort on it has quietly accepted defeat.

passage: The phrase 'guilty pleasure' has become one of the most common ways of talking about taste. A person confesses to loving a televised singing contest, a formulaic romance series or a song that dominated the charts in her teens, and the confession is offered with a smile that asks to be forgiven. On the surface the phrase is modest, even self-deprecating; looked at more closely, it does a surprising amount of work, and not all of that work is modest.

Consider what the speaker gains. By calling the pleasure guilty, she is able to enjoy the thing while signalling that she knows it is beneath her; she occupies the position of the enthusiast and the position of the critic at once. The confession is a kind of insurance: if her listener turns out to share the enthusiasm, nothing is lost; if the listener sneers, she has already sneered first. What looks like an admission of bad taste is therefore, very often, a display of good taste, since only someone who knows the rankings can confess to violating them.

This is why the phrase, for all its apparent humility, tends to preserve the hierarchy it seems to question. Every guilty pleasure implies an innocent one, a set of books, films and songs that may be enjoyed without apology because they are approved. The confession leaves that ranking intact; indeed it needs the ranking in order to mean anything. And the ranking itself is rarely examined. It is striking how often the pleasures labelled guilty are those associated with audiences who have little cultural prestige, the teenage, the provincial, the domestic, while the pleasures of the already respected are seldom described in this way, however predictable they may be.

It does not follow that no pleasure should ever make us uneasy. Some enjoyments really do deserve scrutiny: laughter at another person's humiliation, for instance, or the thrill of watching real suffering staged for entertainment. But in those cases the unease concerns what the pleasure does or endorses, not where its object sits in a ranking of prestige, and the honest response is to ask what we are enjoying and why. That question is worth asking of the singing contest as well. Perhaps the answer will be that it offers something real, the spectacle of ordinary people attempting something difficult in public. If so, the pleasure needs no apology; if not, a shrug and a smile will not settle the matter either.

passage: For a generation, the managers of manufacturing firms were taught to regard inventory as waste. Parts sitting in a warehouse tie up money, take up space and conceal problems that a tighter system would expose, so the ideal was to have each component arrive just as it was needed, often from a single supplier chosen because it was the cheapest or the best. Applied across borders, this logic produced supply chains of remarkable length and precision, in which a product might cross several frontiers as it was assembled, with little stock held at any stage.

The gains were real, and it would be a mistake to dismiss them in hindsight. Lower costs reached consumers as lower prices, and firms in poorer countries gained access to markets they could not otherwise have entered. But a system tuned to perform well under normal conditions can perform very badly under abnormal ones. When a single factory, port or region on which many chains depend is shut by a fire, a flood or a closed border, there is no slack anywhere to absorb the shock, and the shortage of one cheap part can halt the assembly of goods worth thousands of times as much.

A popular response is to call for production to be brought home. The instinct is understandable, but as a remedy for fragility it is oddly chosen. A chain that depends on one domestic plant is no less exposed to a single fire or flood than one that depends on a single foreign plant; it has merely moved its point of failure to a place that feels more familiar. What protects against disruption is not proximity but redundancy: more than one supplier for critical parts, suppliers in places unlikely to suffer the same shock at the same time, and stocks large enough to bridge an interruption.

Redundancy, however, costs money, which is precisely why lean systems eliminated it. A firm deciding how much spare capacity to keep weighs the expense against its own expected losses from a disruption, but some of the losses fall on others: on patients who cannot obtain a medicine, on other firms whose lines stop, on workers sent home without pay. Because these costs do not appear in the firm's accounts, it will tend to hold less insurance than would be sensible for the economy as a whole. The real question, then, is not where things are made but who pays for the resilience that markets left to themselves will tend to supply too sparingly.

passage: Literary history has always been written from a remarkably small sample. Of the many thousands of novels published in a given century, a scholar can read a few hundred in a working life, and the histories of the form are built on a smaller set still, the books that later readers chose to keep in print. When such a history says that 'the novel' turned inward at a certain period, or abandoned the omniscient narrator, or grew preoccupied with the city, it is generalising from a selection that was never meant to be representative. Nobody chose the canon as a sample; it was assembled by generations of readers for reasons of taste, teaching and accident, and there is no reason to expect it to resemble the whole from which it was drawn. The advocates of computational or 'distant' reading start from this embarrassment. If machines can process an entire century's output, counting words, tracking the length of sentences or the frequency with which characters are named, then claims about the form as a whole can at last be tested against the whole.

The objections are familiar, and some are serious. Counting is not reading. The meaning of a word depends on its context, on irony, on the dramatic situation in which it is spoken, none of which a frequency table records. Critics add that many of the patterns such studies report are either trivial or confirm what attentive readers already knew, so that a great deal of machinery produces a modest result dressed in charts. There is also a subtler worry: the features a computer can count are those that can be defined mechanically, and these are not obviously the features that matter. A discipline that adopts such tools risks drifting towards studying what can be measured simply because it can be measured. Defenders of the method reply that every discipline begins by measuring crude things, but the reply concedes more than it denies.

Yet much of this debate rests on a false picture of the choice. Distant reading does not replace close reading so much as change what close reading is asked to do. Its most interesting results are rarely the patterns themselves; they are the anomalies, the decade in which a measure behaves unexpectedly or the obscure novels that cluster with canonical ones on some feature nobody had thought to examine. A measure that shows some habit of style rising steadily for decades and then collapsing within a few years explains nothing by itself, but it tells a scholar exactly where to look. Such a finding means little until someone goes back and reads the books in question, and it is that return which produces understanding. The count poses a question; it does not answer one.

Where the method does make an independent contribution is in the matter of the sample. Even if a computer can say little about what any single novel means, it can show that a generalisation drawn from the canon fails to hold for the much larger body of books that the canon left out. That is not a trivial service. A claim about what 'the novel' did, which turns out to describe only the few hundred books that survived into the syllabus, was never a claim about the novel at all, but about the tastes of the readers who did the selecting. The modest promise of distant reading, then, is less to tell us what literature means than to tell us more accurately which literature our claims are about.

passage: A familiar story about the history of reading holds that, for most of antiquity and much of the Middle Ages, people could read only aloud, and that silent reading was a late discovery which transformed the inner life of the West. The story is usually supported by a much-cited anecdote in which an ancient writer records his surprise at finding a learned man reading without voicing the words. It is a vivid story, and like many vivid stories it has been asked to carry more weight than it can bear.

Scholars who have examined the evidence more closely have found a fair number of ancient readers who read silently, and they point out that surprise at a practice is not evidence that it was unknown, only that it was unusual where it was observed. The more defensible claim is not that silent reading was impossible but that it was not the default. Texts were frequently written without spaces between words, which made voicing them a useful aid, and, more importantly, reading was often a social act. A household, a monastery or a circle of friends would gather while one person read to the others; a book was something one heard as often as something one saw.

What changed, then, was less the technique than the setting. As books became cheaper and more numerous, as spaces between words and other aids to the eye became standard, and as people of moderate means came to have rooms, or at least corners, to themselves, reading moved from the common table to the private chair. Freed from the pace of the voice, the eye could also move faster, and a reader alone could get through more books, and more kinds of book, than a listener ever could. The shift was gradual and uneven, and reading aloud never vanished. Families read novels to one another well into the age of print, and workers in some trades paid a colleague to read to them while they laboured.

Even corrected in this way, the history matters. A text that is heard together is interpreted together: listeners react, object and argue, and the meaning of a passage is settled, if it is settled at all, in company. A text read alone is answerable only to its reader, who may skip, reread or linger over a sentence that no one else will ever know about. It would be too much to say that private reading created the private self. It would be too little to say that it changed nothing about how people came to think of their thoughts as their own.

passage: Introducing video review into professional sport seemed to settle an old grievance. For as long as games have had officials, players and spectators have complained that decisions were wrong, and now there was a technology that could show, from several angles and at any speed, what had really happened. Few people expected that the result would be a new and more corrosive kind of dispute. Yet that is what many supporters now describe: arguments that once ended with the whistle continue through slow-motion replays, frozen frames and lines drawn on screens, and they seem less settled than before.

The puzzle dissolves once we ask what the referee's authority was for. It was never simply a matter of being right. A match needs some means of converting a contested event into a settled fact quickly enough for play to continue, and the referee supplied it by being final. Players accepted decisions they believed mistaken not because they trusted the official's eyesight but because they had accepted, in joining the game, that someone must decide and that the decision would stand. Error was tolerated as the price of finality, and since the errors fell, over a season, on all sides alike, the price seemed bearable.

Review alters this bargain in two ways. First, it relocates authority. The decision now seems to belong to the replay, and the referee on the field becomes a provisional judge whose rulings await confirmation from elsewhere. Second, and less obviously, it changes the kind of question being asked. Whether a challenge was reckless, or whether an attacker gained an advantage, is a matter of judgement that a trained official can make in a moment. Whether a toe was ahead of a defender's shoulder at the instant the ball was struck is presented as a matter of fact, yet the answer depends on which frame is chosen and where the line is drawn, choices that the apparent precision of the image conceals. A decision dressed as measurement invites challenge in a way that an acknowledged judgement does not, because every measurement can be disputed by another.

None of this is a case for abandoning the cameras. A goal awarded for a shot that plainly missed, or a player sent off for a foul committed by someone else, is an injustice that no appeal to finality can make acceptable, and replays remove such errors cheaply. The mistake lies in treating review as a means of perfecting every marginal call. Confined to clear and obvious errors, it supports the referee's authority; extended to the margins, it dissolves the very finality that made officiating possible.
